category: Reporting with attitude: complaining, boasting, apologizing

entries.patterns: accuse + sb / accuse + sb + of + -ing / accuse + sb + of + noun phrase / accuse + sb + of + having done sth / passive be accused of
entries.never: accuse someone that they did something / accuse someone for doing something / accuse someone to have done something
entries.meaning: A charge of wrongdoing laid at a named person, and it presupposes that the accuser believes the offense real. Compare blame, which assigns responsibility for an outcome without necessarily alleging misconduct, and criticize, which faults a choice rather than charging an offense.
entries.transform: "You took the money," she said to him. -> She accused him of taking the money.
examples: She accused her landlord of ignoring three written repair requests.
He accused me of leaking the memo, which I hadn't.
Two former employees have accused the company of retaliation.
Nobody was accusing anyone of anything — they just wanted the numbers explained.
"Don't accuse me of something you can't prove," he said.
The report stops short of accusing the department of misconduct.

entries.patterns: identical to apologize — apologise (intransitive) / apologise + to sb / apologise + for + -ing / apologise + for + noun phrase / apologise + to sb + for + -ing / noun phrase
entries.never: apologise me / apologise him for the delay / apologise in an American text — American English requires apologize
entries.meaning: The same speech act as apologize — nothing about the meaning or the grammar changes with the spelling.
entries.transform: "Sorry I'm late," he said. -> He apologised for being late. (British)
examples: The minister apologised to the families for the delay in the inquiry. (British press)
Our style guide uses apologise, so the American draft had to be respelled throughout.
She apologised for the confusion and reissued the invoice. (British)
Both apologise and apologize appear in the OED; only one appears in Merriam-Webster's main entry.
He never learned which spelling his company used, so he wrote I'm sorry instead.
The autocorrect kept changing apologise to apologize, which told him what dictionary it was using.

entries.patterns: apologize (intransitive) / apologize + to sb / apologize + for + -ing / apologize + for + noun phrase / apologize + to sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / apologize + that-clause (institutional only, see below)
entries.never: apologize me / apologize him for the delay / apologize about the delay / apologized the customer for the delay / apologized for the delay to the customer
entries.meaning: An expression of regret for one's own act, which presupposes fault the way admit and confess do. It is not the same as expressing sympathy — you apologize for what you did, and you say I'm sorry for what merely happened.
entries.transform: "I'm sorry I snapped at you," he said. -> He apologized for snapping at me.
examples: He apologized to the whole team for missing the deadline.
She apologized for the confusion and sent a corrected schedule.
I'm not going to apologize for wanting the contract in writing.
The airline apologized profusely and gave everyone a voucher.
"You could at least apologize," she said, and he did.
He apologized to her, not to me, which was the whole problem.

entries.patterns: blame + sb / blame + sb + for + -ing / blame + sb + for + noun phrase / blame + oneself + for / blame + sth + on + sb / blame + noun phrase (blame the weather) / be to blame (for)
entries.never: blame someone of something / blame someone about something / He blamed that the driver was speeding
entries.meaning: The assignment of responsibility for something bad. Unlike accuse, it need allege no misconduct — you can blame the weather, the software, or bad luck — and unlike criticize, it targets an outcome rather than a judgment call.
entries.transform: "It's your fault the server went down," she said. -> She blamed me for the outage. / She blamed the outage on me.
examples: Don't blame the intern — nobody told her the file was live.
He blamed the loss on a single bad call in the third quarter.
She blamed herself for not catching the typo before it printed.
I don't blame you for walking out of that meeting.
The report blames poor maintenance for the failure.
Everyone knew who was to blame, and nobody said it out loud.

entries.patterns: boast + that-clause / boast + about + -ing / noun / boast + of + -ing / noun / boast + to sb + that / about / boast + noun phrase (only in the "possess proudly" sense) / + direct quotation
entries.never: boast someone that / boast to do something / He boasted to have won
entries.meaning: A claim advanced with self-satisfaction. Boast is the least loaded of the four self-praise verbs — it can be neutral or even admiring (boasts a spotless record) — where brag is informal and disapproving, crow is loud, and gloat requires someone else's loss.
entries.transform: "I've never lost a case," he said. -> He boasted that he had never lost a case.
examples: He boasted that he could fix the transmission in an afternoon.
She never boasts about the awards; you have to find out from someone else.
They boasted of a turnaround time no competitor could match.
The résumé boasted fifteen years of experience she did not have.
"I boast," he admitted, "but only about things I've actually done."
The new terminal boasts the shortest security lines in the region.

entries.patterns: brag + that-clause / brag + about + -ing / noun / brag + of + -ing / noun (much rarer than with boast) / brag + to sb + about / that / + direct quotation
entries.never: brag something / He bragged his salary / brag
entries.meaning: The same act as boast but with the disapproval built in. Calling it bragging is itself a judgment; no one describes their own speech that way except jokingly (not to brag, but…), which is the standard American hedge for bragging anyway.
entries.transform: "I closed four deals this week," he said. -> He bragged that he had closed four deals that week.
examples: He bragged that he'd never once been late to work.
Stop bragging about the truck — everyone has seen it.
She bragged to her sister about getting the corner office.
Not to brag, but I fixed the sink myself.
The kids bragged all afternoon about who caught the bigger fish.
He brags less now that people know what the numbers actually were.

entries.patterns: chide + sb / chide + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / + direct quotation ("You promised," she chided) / passive be chided for
entries.never: chide someone that they did something / chide someone to do something / chide at someone
entries.meaning: A mild, often affectionate rebuke — the gentlest verb in the scold–rebuke–reproach family, and the only one that can be teasing. It reads as bookish; in speech an American would say gave him a hard time or ribbed him.
entries.transform: "You really should have called," she said. -> She chided him for not calling.
examples: She chided him for showing up empty-handed, but she was smiling.
The columnist chided the mayor for reading a statement instead of answering.
"You're impossible," she chided, and handed him the umbrella anyway.
He was chided more than punished, which suited him fine.
Her grandmother chided her for speaking English at the dinner table.
The editorial chided both parties for walking away from the table.

entries.patterns: complain + that-clause / complain + about + noun phrase / -ing / complain + of + noun phrase / -ing / complain + to sb + about / of / that / complain (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: complain me / complain the manager about the noise / complain something / She complained the noise / complained about that the food was cold
entries.meaning: A statement of dissatisfaction, usually addressed to someone who might fix it — which is what separates it from grumble and gripe, where nobody expects redress.
entries.transform: "The heat hasn't worked in three days," she said. -> She complained that the heat hadn't worked in three days.
examples: Three tenants complained that the elevator had been out since Friday.
He complained to HR about the scheduling, and nothing changed.
She came in complaining of a headache and a stiff neck.
Passengers complained about being kept on the tarmac for two hours.
"I'm not complaining," he said, complaining.
Nobody complained, which the manager took as approval.

entries.patterns: compliment + sb / compliment + sb + on + noun phrase / -ing / passive be complimented on
entries.never: compliment someone that they did well / complimented her for her presentation
entries.meaning: A short, direct expression of admiration said to the person's face. Praise can be public and about a third party; a compliment is addressed to its target.
entries.transform: "That was a great presentation," he said to her. -> He complimented her on her presentation.
examples: He complimented her on the way she handled the hostile question.
Nobody had ever complimented his handwriting before.
She complimented the cook and asked for the recipe.
I was complimented on my Spanish by someone who had heard four words of it.
"Was that a compliment?" "It was supposed to be."
He complimented the team publicly and criticized them in private.

entries.patterns: condemn + noun phrase / condemn + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / condemn + sb / sth + as + noun phrase / adjective / passive be condemned (as / for) / condemn + sb + to + noun phrase (= sentence — a separate sense)
entries.never: condemn that the policy was unfair / condemn someone of something / condemned him to lie
entries.meaning: The strongest public denunciation in this group. Where criticize faults a decision and accuse charges an offense, condemn declares the thing morally unacceptable, which is why it is the standard verb of diplomatic statements.
entries.transform: "This attack is unacceptable and we reject it," the statement said. -> The government condemned the attack.
examples: Both senators condemned the ruling within the hour.
The union condemned the layoffs as a breach of the agreement.
She condemned the practice for putting drivers at risk.
The report stops at describing the failures; it does not condemn anyone.
"I condemn it in the strongest possible terms," he said, which meant nothing would happen.
The building was condemned, in the other sense, six months later.

entries.patterns: congratulate + sb / congratulate + sb + on + noun phrase / -ing / congratulate + oneself + on / passive be congratulated on
entries.never: congratulate your promotion / congratulated me that I had passed
entries.meaning: An acknowledgment of someone's good fortune or achievement. It does not evaluate the person's work, which is what separates it from praise and compliment — you can congratulate someone on a lottery win.
entries.transform: "Congratulations on the new job!" she said. -> She congratulated me on the new job.
examples: She congratulated the whole team on shipping two weeks early.
He congratulated his opponent and left the stage without another word.
I congratulated her on the baby before I realized she hadn't announced it.
They congratulated themselves on a decision that had mostly been luck.
"Am I supposed to congratulate you?" she asked, not warmly.
The email congratulated everyone on numbers that three people had actually produced.

entries.patterns: identical to criticize — criticise + sb / sth / criticise + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / criticise + sb / sth + as + adjective / noun phrase / passive be criticised for
entries.never: criticise me that I was late / criticise in an American text — American English requires criticize
entries.meaning: Exactly what criticize reports. The entry exists so the spelling can be recognized in British sources and then not copied.
entries.transform: "The rollout was badly planned," she said. (British) -> She criticised the rollout as badly planned.
examples: (British usage) The committee criticised the department for its handling of the contract.
(British usage) He was criticised in the press for a remark he never made.
(British usage) The paper criticised the ruling as an extraordinary overreach.
In American English all three of those sentences take criticized, with no other change.
Our house style is British, so every criticize in the draft was respelled criticise.
Both spellings appear in the OED; only criticize heads the Merriam-Webster entry.

entries.patterns: criticize + sb / sth / criticize + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / criticize + sb / sth + as + adjective / noun phrase / passive be criticized for / be criticized as
entries.never: criticize about the delay / criticize that the plan was rushed / criticized me that I was late
entries.meaning: An unfavorable judgment of a choice, a performance, or a piece of work. Weaker than condemn, broader than accuse — you can criticize something without alleging any wrongdoing at all, and academic criticism is not even negative.
entries.transform: "The rollout was badly planned and you knew it," she said. -> She criticized the rollout as badly planned.
examples: Two board members criticized the timing but voted for it anyway.
She was criticized for saying out loud what everyone had written down.
The design was criticized as expensive and hard to maintain.
He doesn't take criticism well, which is why nobody criticizes him.
It's easy to criticize a schedule you didn't have to build.
The review criticized the pacing and praised almost everything else.

entries.patterns: crow + that-clause / crow + about + noun phrase / -ing / crow + over + noun phrase / -ing / crow + to sb + that / about / + direct quotation
entries.never: crow something / crow someone that / crow of the win
entries.meaning: Boasting loudly and publicly, with the metaphor of a rooster fully alive in it — the verb implies noise and an audience. Crow over something specifically means gloating about a victory in front of the loser, which is gloat's territory.
entries.transform: "We beat them by twenty points!" he said, over and over. -> He crowed that they had beaten them by twenty points.
examples: He crowed about the promotion until even his friends stopped answering.
The press release crowed that the company had doubled its market share.
She won the bet and did not crow, which he noticed.
They were still crowing over the takeover three years later.
"Don't crow until the check clears," his partner said.
The mayor crowed about a crime drop that had started under his predecessor.

entries.patterns: cry + direct quotation (with or without inversion: "Stop!" she cried / "Stop!" cried the guard) / cry + that-clause (literary) / cry out + that-clause / cry out + to sb (+ that / to-infinitive) / cry + for + noun phrase (cried for help) / cry (intransitive — weep)
entries.never: cry someone that / cry someone something
entries.meaning: A loud, sudden utterance driven by emotion — alarm, protest, delight. Compare exclaim, which is formal but not loud, and shout, which is loud but carries no literary flavor.
entries.transform: "Look out!" she said suddenly. -> She cried a warning. / "Look out!" she cried.
examples: "Cry all you want," he said, "but the deposit is nonrefundable."
"There's someone in the water!" she cried.
He cried out that the ladder was slipping.
The crowd cried for a recount and got one.
She read the last page twice and then cried.
"Not one more word," cried the judge, in a novel nobody would publish now.

entries.patterns: exclaim + direct quotation / exclaim + that-clause / exclaim + to sb + that / exclaim + over / at + noun phrase / wh-clause (= react admiringly or with dismay)
entries.never: exclaim someone that / exclaim something / She exclaimed her surprise
entries.meaning: A sudden utterance made under strong feeling, usually surprise or delight. Unlike cry it need not be loud, and unlike shout it says nothing about volume at all.
entries.transform: "I can't believe you're here!" she said. -> She exclaimed that she couldn't believe I was there.
examples: "You're kidding!" she exclaimed, and put down her fork.
He exclaimed that he had never seen anything like it.
The guests exclaimed over the cake for a solid five minutes.
"Exclaimed" appears eleven times in the first chapter, which is nine too many.
She exclaimed at the price and bought it anyway.
"At last!" exclaimed the letter, in capitals, with three exclamation points.

entries.patterns: gloat + that-clause / gloat + about / over + noun phrase / -ing / gloat + to sb (+ that / about) / gloat (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: gloat something / gloat someone / gloat of the result
entries.meaning: Open, undisguised pleasure in one's own success or — the core sense — in someone else's misfortune. This is the only verb in the boasting family that requires a loser. Boast and brag need only a winner; gloat needs a defeat to enjoy.
entries.transform: "I told you it wouldn't work," she said, smiling. -> She gloated that she had told me it wouldn't work.
examples: He gloated for a week about winning a game of cards.
She gloated that the forecast she'd been mocked for had turned out right.
Try not to gloat in front of the people who lost their jobs.
There was no gloating in the locker room, just relief.
"I'm not gloating," he said, gloating.
The rival paper gloated over the correction for two full editorials.

entries.patterns: gripe + that-clause / gripe + about + noun phrase / -ing / gripe + to sb + about / that / gripe + at sb (informal, on the grumble model) / gripe (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: gripe someone / gripe something / griped me the schedule
entries.meaning: Low-grade, habitual complaining to someone who cannot fix it — the American workplace verb for it. Nearly identical to grumble but blunter and more colloquial; a gripe as a noun is a specific grievance (my one gripe is the parking), which grumble does not do as naturally.
entries.transform: "These shifts are impossible," he said to his coworker. -> He griped to his coworker about the shifts.
examples: They griped about the new time-tracking software for a month, then learned it.
He griped to me that nobody had told him the meeting moved.
My only gripe with the place is that it's loud.
Stop griping and file the ticket.
She gripes constantly and still hasn't missed a shift in six years.
There was plenty of griping in the parking lot and none in the room.

entries.type: reporting verb — complaint, manner of speaking
entries.patterns: groan + direct quotation / groan + that-clause / groan + about + noun phrase / -ing / groan + to sb (+ that) / groan + at + noun phrase (= react to: groaned at the price) / groan (intransitive) / groan + noun phrase (rare: groaned an apology)
entries.never: groan someone / groan someone that
entries.meaning: A low, drawn-out sound of pain, exhaustion, or dismay — and, by extension, the complaint that comes out with it. The that-clause is fully idiomatic here (he groaned that his back was killing him), unlike sigh, because a groan can carry words.
entries.transform: "Oh no, not another form," he said. -> He groaned that there was another form.
examples: The whole class groaned when she announced a pop quiz.
He groaned that he'd left his wallet in the other jacket.
She groaned, rolled over, and hit snooze again.
There was a collective groan from the back of the room.
"Not the highway at five," he groaned.
The old stairs groaned under the weight of the piano.

entries.patterns: growl + direct quotation / growl + that-clause / growl + at sb / growl + at sb + to-infinitive (growled at me to move) / growl + noun phrase (growled an order) / growl (intransitive)
entries.never: growl someone something / He growled me a warning
entries.meaning: Speech delivered low in the throat with hostility or menace. It is a fiction verb: real reports say said angrily. Growl at someone is aggressive; growl + quotation is simply a description of the voice.
entries.transform: "Get out of my chair," he said, very low. -> He growled at me to get out of his chair.
examples: "Try it," he growled, and nobody tried it.
The dog growled at the mail carrier through the screen door.
She growled that she had asked for the report twice already.
He growled an answer without looking up from the engine.
The coach growled at the bench and the bench got quiet.
His stomach growled loudly enough that the interviewer laughed.

entries.patterns: grumble + that-clause / grumble + about + noun phrase / -ing / grumble + to sb + about / that / grumble + at sb / grumble (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: grumble someone / grumble something
entries.meaning: Continuous, half-audible complaining that expects nothing to change. Complain is addressed to someone who might act; grumble is muttered sideways. It is also the standard verb for low-level institutional discontent: staff grumbled about the new policy.
entries.transform: "This is the third reorg in two years," she said under her breath. -> She grumbled that it was the third reorg in two years.
examples: He grumbled about the parking every single morning for eleven years.
Several senators grumbled that they had seen the bill only that morning.
She paid the fee, grumbling, and kept the receipt.
There was some grumbling in the ranks and no actual objection.
"Fine," he grumbled, and picked up the other end of the couch.
They grumbled to each other in the hallway and said nothing in the meeting.

entries.patterns: joke + that-clause / joke + about + noun phrase / -ing / joke + with sb + about / that / joke (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: joke someone that / joke something / joked the crowd
entries.meaning: A remark made in fun, and joke that is the standard journalistic frame for reporting a quip while signaling that the speaker did not mean it literally. That signal matters: He said he'd quit and He joked that he'd quit describe the same words and opposite situations.
entries.transform: "At this rate I'll retire before the permit comes through," he said, laughing. -> He joked that he would retire before the permit came through.
examples: She joked that the coffee machine had a better attendance record than she did.
He joked about his accent before anyone else could.
They joked with the security guard while the alarm was being reset.
I was joking, and about half the room knew it.
You can't joke about that in a deposition.
He joked that he'd be fine, which is how everyone missed how bad it was.

entries.patterns: lament + that-clause / lament + noun phrase / lament + the fact that / lament + over / for + noun phrase (literary, = mourn) / lament (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: lament about something / lamented me that / lamented to have lost the house
entries.meaning: Grief or regret expressed publicly, usually about something already lost and beyond fixing. That is the difference from complain: a complaint asks for a remedy, a lament concedes there is none. It is a written verb — in speech Americans say was upset about or kept saying how sad it was.
entries.transform: "There's nowhere left in this town to buy a book," she said. -> She lamented that there was nowhere left in town to buy a book.
examples: The editorial laments the disappearance of the local paper it competes with.
She lamented that none of her students had read a newspaper that week.
He lamented the state of the roads to anyone who would listen.
The song laments a river that no longer runs.
Critics lamented the ending and praised everything before it.
There is no point lamenting a deadline you already missed.

entries.patterns: laugh (intransitive) / laugh + direct quotation / laugh + at + sb / sth / laugh + about / over + noun phrase / -ing / laugh + off + noun phrase / laugh + that-clause (disputed — see below)
entries.never: laugh someone / laugh someone for doing something
entries.meaning: Amusement, real or performed. As a reporting verb it usually says how something was said rather than what act it was.
entries.transform: "It's fine, honestly," she said, laughing. -> She laughed and said it was fine.
examples: She laughed when she saw the size of the invoice.
They laughed about the wrong turn for the rest of the drive.
Don't laugh — I got the last two parking spots on the block.
He laughed off a question he should have answered.
Nobody laughed, which told him the joke had landed wrong.
"You'll laugh," she said, and we did not.

entries.type: reporting verb — complaint, manner of speaking
entries.patterns: moan + that-clause / moan + about + noun phrase / -ing / moan + to sb + about / that / moan + direct quotation / moan (intransitive) / moan + at sb (British)
entries.never: moan someone / moan something / moaned me about the heat
entries.meaning: A long low sound, or the complaint delivered in that tone. Softer and more drawn out than groan, which is shorter and lower.
entries.transform: "It's so hot in here I can't think," she said. -> She moaned about the heat.
examples: He moaned about the commute until he moved four blocks from the office.
She moaned that she'd been on hold for forty minutes.
The wind moaned in the chimney all night.
Stop moaning — you picked the restaurant.
He moaned softly and asked for more ice.
There's no point moaning about a rule you voted for.

entries.patterns: mock + sb / sth / mock + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / mock + sb's accent / voice / walk / + direct quotation delivered in imitation / passive be mocked for
entries.never: mock at someone / mocked at him / mocked that he was scared
entries.meaning: Ridicule aimed at making someone look foolish, usually by imitation. Unlike tease it is not affectionate, and unlike criticize it attacks the person rather than the choice. Mock- as a prefix (mock trial, mock-serious) means "imitation," which is the same root doing honest work.
entries.transform: "Ooh, look at me, I read the manual," he said in a high voice. -> He mocked me for reading the manual.
examples: He mocked the accent for a full minute before noticing whose family had it.
She was mocked online for a typo in a two-line post.
Don't mock the checklist — the checklist is why the plane lands.
They mocked his handwriting and copied his answers.
The bill was mocked by both parties and passed unanimously.
"Are you mocking me?" "A little."

entries.patterns: mumble + direct quotation / mumble + that-clause / mumble + noun phrase (mumbled an apology) / mumble + to sb (+ that) / mumble + something about + noun / mumble (intransitive)
entries.never: mumble me something / mumbled me something
entries.meaning: Speech produced so indistinctly that the words are hard to make out — a fact about articulation, not about mood. That is what separates it from mutter, which is clear enough but resentful, and murmur, which is soft but usually warm. You can mumble a compliment.
entries.transform: "Sorry, I didn't see it," he said, barely audibly. -> He mumbled that he hadn't seen it.
examples: He mumbled an apology and went back to his desk.
She mumbled that she'd finish it by Friday, and she did.
Stop mumbling — the microphone is right there.
The witness mumbled through the oath and had to repeat it.
He mumbled something to the cashier that neither of them understood.
Teenagers mumble; it is not a moral failing.

entries.patterns: murmur + direct quotation / murmur + that-clause / murmur + noun phrase (murmured her name) / murmur + to sb / to oneself (+ that) / murmur (intransitive)
entries.never: murmur someone something / murmur at someone
entries.meaning: Soft, low speech, usually gentle, intimate, or approving — the warm member of the quiet-speech family. Where mutter is resentful and mumble is unclear, a murmur is deliberately quiet and perfectly articulate. There is also a collective sense: a murmur ran through the crowd, meaning a low general sound of reaction.
entries.transform: "It's going to be all right," she said very softly. -> She murmured that it was going to be all right.
examples: She murmured something to the nurse and squeezed his hand.
The audience murmured when the lights came back up.
He murmured that he'd rather not discuss it in the hallway.
A murmur of agreement went around the table.
"Stay," she murmured, and he stayed.
The stream murmured through the whole recording, which ruined the take.

entries.type: reporting verb — manner of speaking, complaint
entries.patterns: mutter + direct quotation / mutter + that-clause / mutter + noun phrase (muttered a curse) / mutter + about + noun phrase / -ing / mutter + to sb / to oneself (+ that) / mutter (intransitive)
entries.never: mutter someone that
entries.meaning: Low, half-audible speech carrying resentment — words the speaker wants heard just enough to register and not enough to answer. That resentment is the whole difference from mumble: a mumble is unclear by accident, a mutter is quiet on purpose.
entries.transform: "This is a complete waste of time," he said under his breath. -> He muttered that it was a complete waste of time.
examples: He muttered something about the budget and left the room.
She muttered that she'd been asking for that data since March.
He walks the halls muttering to himself and writes the best code in the building.
"Say it out loud or don't mutter it," his father said.
There was muttering in the back row for the rest of the presentation.
She muttered a word her grandmother would not have approved of.

entries.patterns: object + that-clause / object + to + noun phrase / object + to + -ing / object + to + sb('s) + -ing (objected to my leaving early) / object (intransitive) / + direct quotation
entries.never: object to be treated that way / object something / object against
entries.meaning: A stated disagreement, usually procedural or principled rather than emotional. It is the formal end of the complaining family — the courtroom verb, the meeting verb — where complain is domestic and protest is louder and more self-defensive.
entries.transform: "I don't think we should vote on this today," she said. -> She objected to voting on it that day.
examples: Two members objected to the wording and one objected to the whole idea.
She objected that no one had seen the contract before the meeting.
If nobody objects, we'll move to the next item.
He objected to being asked the same question a third time.
"Objection," said the attorney, and the judge sustained it.
I don't object in principle; I object to the timing.

entries.patterns: praise + sb / sth / praise + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / praise + sb / sth + as + noun phrase / adjective / passive be praised for / be praised as
entries.never: praise someone that they did well / praise about something
entries.meaning: Approval expressed publicly, and unlike compliment it need not be said to the person's face or even in their hearing: the review praised the second act. It evaluates the work, where congratulate merely acknowledges the outcome.
entries.transform: "She handled that better than anyone could have," he said. -> He praised her for her handling of it.
examples: The inspector praised the crew for stopping work when they noticed the crack.
She was praised in public and passed over in private.
The review praised the cinematography and said nothing about the plot.
He praises people specifically, which is why it means something.
Faint praise is worse than none.
Both papers praised the settlement as a reasonable compromise.

entries.patterns: protest + that-clause / protest + noun phrase (American) / protest + against / at + noun phrase (British) / protest + to sb (+ that) / protest + direct quotation / protest (intransitive) / protest + noun phrase (= assert: protested his innocence)
entries.never: protest to do something / protest someone that / protested the referee that
entries.meaning: A stated objection to something perceived as unjust, often self-defensive and often after the fact. "But I didn't touch it!" he protested is the characteristic use — the verb carries a hint that the objection may not be believed, which is why he protested his innocence is always faintly skeptical.
entries.transform: "But I turned it in on Tuesday!" he said. -> He protested that he had turned it in on Tuesday.
examples: Students protested the tuition increase for three weeks.
"I never agreed to that," she protested.
He protested that he had asked twice and gotten no answer.
She protested her innocence right up to the plea deal.
Thousands protested outside the statehouse in the rain.
He signed it under protest and said so in writing.

entries.patterns: rebuke + sb / rebuke + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / passive be rebuked for / noun a rebuke (to sb)
entries.never: rebuke someone that they were late / rebuke someone to do something / rebuke at someone
entries.meaning: A sharp, formal reprimand delivered by someone with standing to deliver it — a court, a board, a superior. Stronger and more official than chide, less domestic than scold, and unlike criticize it is an act of authority rather than an opinion. In American news writing it most often appears in the passive or as a noun: a sharp rebuke from the bench.
entries.transform: "This filing is unacceptable and you know better," the judge said. -> The judge rebuked the attorney for the filing.
examples: The committee rebuked two of its own members and expelled neither.
He was publicly rebuked for comments he made at a fundraiser.
The ruling is a rebuke to every agency that assumed the rule was optional.
She rebuked the staff for a leak nobody could trace.
The letter rebuked the department in language unusual for an inspector general.
A quiet rebuke from her did more than an hour of shouting from him.

entries.patterns: reproach + sb / reproach + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / reproach + sb + with + noun phrase (formal) / reproach + oneself + for / passive be reproached for / noun a reproach, above reproach
entries.never: reproach someone that they forgot / reproach at someone
entries.meaning: Disappointed criticism delivered to someone you had expectations of — the hurt cousin of rebuke. Where a rebuke asserts authority, a reproach asserts a relationship, which is why she reproached him implies they knew each other and she rebuked him does not.
entries.transform: "I thought you of all people would have said something," she said. -> She reproached him for staying quiet.
examples: She reproached him for missing the funeral and never mentioned it again.
He reproached himself for years over a decision that was never his to make.
Her record is above reproach, which is why the accusation landed so oddly.
The letter reproached the board with its own published standards.
There was more sorrow than anger in the reproach.
Nobody reproached the intern; everyone reproached the manager.

entries.patterns: scold + sb / scold + sb + for + -ing / noun phrase / + direct quotation ("Not on the couch," she scolded) / passive be scolded for
entries.never: scold someone that they did it / scold someone to do something / scold at someone
entries.meaning: An angry telling-off, prototypically an adult to a child. Using it of two adults is a deliberate move — she scolded her colleague makes the colleague sound infantilized, which is sometimes exactly the point and is a well-known trap in reporting on women in public life.
entries.transform: "How many times have I told you not to slam that door?" -> She scolded him for slamming the door.
examples: She scolded the dog, who was unmoved.
He was scolded by a stranger for parking across two spaces.
"Inside voices," she scolded, without looking up.
The op-ed scolds readers for a problem it spends no words explaining.
My grandmother scolded me in two languages, for emphasis.
Nobody likes being scolded by a machine, which is why the warning gets ignored.

entries.patterns: shout + direct quotation / shout + that-clause / shout + wh-clause / shout + noun phrase (shouted an order) / shout + at sb / shout + to sb / shout + at/to sb + to-infinitive / shout (intransitive)
entries.never: shout someone that / shout someone something / shouted me that
entries.meaning: Loud speech. Unlike yell it is not necessarily angry, and unlike cry it carries no literary flavor.
entries.transform: "The bridge is out!" he said at the top of his voice. -> He shouted that the bridge was out.
examples: Someone shouted that the elevator was stuck between floors.
He shouted to her across the parking lot and she didn't hear him.
Please stop shouting at the umpire; he has a hard enough job.
She shouted over the music to ask where the bathroom was.
He shouted a warning about half a second before the shelf came down.
They shouted until they were hoarse and the vote went the other way anyway.

entries.patterns: sigh (intransitive) / sigh + direct quotation / sigh + that-clause (fiction) / sigh + over / about + noun phrase / -ing / sigh + for + noun phrase (literary, = long for) / noun a sigh, with a sigh
entries.never: sigh someone / sigh someone that
entries.meaning: Resignation, weariness, or relief expressed as breath. As a reporting verb it tells you the speaker had given up, not what act was performed.
entries.transform: "All right, I'll do it myself," she said wearily. -> She sighed that she would do it herself. / She said with a sigh that she would do it herself.
examples: She sighed, looked at the clock, and opened the file again.
"There's nothing else to try," he sighed.
He sighed over the invoice for a while and then paid it.
There was a long sigh on the other end of the line.
The whole room sighed with relief when the numbers came up green.
She sighed that she'd been through three of these reorganizations already.

entries.type: reporting verb — manner of speaking, irritation
entries.patterns: snap + direct quotation / snap + that-clause / snap + at sb / snap + at sb + to-infinitive (snapped at him to sit down) / snap (intransitive, = lose one's temper)
entries.never: snap someone / snap someone that / snap to someone
entries.meaning: A short, sharp, irritated reply — brevity is the whole point. A snapped remark is one sentence, delivered in a tone that ends the exchange. Compare mutter, which is resentful but quiet, and yell, which is loud but not necessarily short.
entries.transform: "I said I'd handle it," she said sharply. -> She snapped that she had said she'd handle it.
examples: "I'm not asking again," he snapped.
She snapped that she'd sent the file twice already.
Sorry I snapped at you — it's been a long week.
He snapped at a waiter and the whole table went quiet.
She almost never snaps, which is why it registered.
He snapped after the third schedule change and walked out.

entries.type: reporting verb — contempt, manner of speaking
entries.patterns: sneer (intransitive) / sneer + at + sb / sth / sneer + that-clause / + direct quotation ("Nice try," he sneered) / noun a sneer, adjective sneering
entries.never: sneer someone / sneer someone that / sneer to someone / sneer about something
entries.meaning: Contempt carried in the voice or the face — a remark delivered as though the thing said were beneath the speaker. Like whine, it is the reporter's verdict rather than a neutral description: he sneered that the plan wouldn't work instructs the reader to dislike him, and a fair report writes said dismissively instead. Compare mock, which works by imitation, and taunt, which works by provocation; a sneer needs no audience beyond the person it dismisses.
entries.transform: "That's the best you could do?" he said, with his lip curled. -> He sneered at my draft.
examples: He sneered at the suggestion that anyone had asked his opinion.
She sneered that the report had been written by someone who had never seen the site.
"Amateurs," he sneered, and went back to his phone.
The column sneers at the readers it is trying to persuade, which is why it persuades nobody.
There was a sneer in his voice that the transcript does not record.
Don't sneer — half of that code is still running in production.

entries.patterns: taunt + sb / taunt + sb + about + noun phrase / -ing / taunt + sb + with + noun phrase / taunt + sb + for + -ing (less common than about) / + direct quotation ("Can't catch me," he taunted) / passive be taunted about / with / noun a taunt
entries.never: taunt at someone / taunt someone that
entries.meaning: Repeated, provoking mockery meant to get a reaction — the playground and the sideline verb. Mock makes someone look foolish; a taunt is designed to make them respond, which is why it is the word used for what starts fights.
entries.transform: "Zero for four! Zero for four!" the fans said, over and over. -> The fans taunted him about going zero for four.
examples: He taunted the goalie for the entire third period.
She taunted him about the bet until he doubled it.
The taunts from the away section got the game stopped for four minutes.
Don't taunt a system administrator two days before your renewal.
They taunted each other cheerfully for an hour and left as friends.
He was taunted with a nickname he'd been given in the seventh grade.

entries.patterns: tease + sb / tease + sb + about + noun phrase / -ing / tease + sb + for + -ing / tease + sb + into / out of + -ing / + direct quotation / passive be teased about
entries.never: tease at someone / tease someone that
entries.meaning: Joking at someone's expense, usually affectionately and usually between people who like each other. That affection is the whole difference from mock and taunt; I was only teasing is the standard American repair when the affection did not come through.
entries.transform: "Nice haircut. Did you lose a bet?" -> She teased him about his haircut.
examples: His sisters teased him about the truck for twenty years.
She teased me for alphabetizing the spice rack.
"I'm teasing," he said, a beat too late.
He was teased mercilessly and gave as good as he got.
She teased him into trying the karaoke machine.
There's a line between teasing and something else, and it moves depending on who's laughing.

entries.patterns: thank + sb / thank + sb + for + noun phrase / thank + sb + for + -ing / thank + sb + for + having done sth / passive be thanked for / fixed idiom I'll thank you to + verb (= a sharp request, not a thanks)
entries.never: thank to someone / thank someone that they came / thank someone of something / thanked to me / thanked me that I came
entries.meaning: An expression of gratitude. This is the verb that turns "Thank you so much for coming" into a single reported clause, and the for + -ing frame is the most reliably useful pattern in this whole file.
entries.transform: "Thank you for covering my shift," he said. -> He thanked me for covering his shift.
examples: She thanked every member of the crew by name.
He thanked me for the ride and I hadn't even offered yet.
I want to thank whoever refilled the coffee at 6 a.m.
They were thanked in the acknowledgments and paid in nothing else.
Don't thank me — thank the person who caught it in review.
She thanked him for his honesty in a tone that suggested otherwise.

entries.patterns: whine + that-clause / whine + about + noun phrase / -ing / whine + to sb + about / that / whine + at + sb / sth (literal noise: whined at the door) / whine + direct quotation / whine (intransitive)
entries.never: whine someone / whine something / whined me about the seat
entries.meaning: Complaining in a high, drawn-out, childish tone — and, crucially, the reporter's verdict that the complaint is unwarranted. There is no neutral use. He complained that the shift was unsafe takes the complaint seriously; He whined that the shift was unsafe dismisses it, which makes this a verb to choose deliberately and never by accident in a report you want read as fair.
entries.transform: "Why do I always have to be the one to close?" -> He whined about always having to close.
examples: He whined about the seating chart until they moved him.
She whined that nobody had told her, though the email was in her inbox.
Stop whining and get in the car.
The dog whined at the door for ten minutes.
Calling it whining was how the complaint got buried.
There's a difference between raising an issue and whining, and it is mostly tone.

entries.patterns: whisper + direct quotation / whisper + that-clause / whisper + wh-clause / whisper + noun phrase (whispered a name) / whisper + to sb + that / whisper + to sb + to-infinitive (whispered to me to wait) / whisper (intransitive) / passive it is whispered that (= rumor)
entries.never: whisper someone that / whisper someone something / whispered me that
entries.meaning: Speech with no voicing behind it, produced quietly on purpose — for secrecy, for intimacy, or because the room requires it. It is the manner verb that most freely takes a that-clause; nobody objects to she whispered that she'd be right back.
entries.transform: "Don't look now, but he's right behind you," she said very quietly. -> She whispered that he was right behind me.
examples: She whispered something to the bailiff and the judge called a recess.
He whispered that the second door was unlocked.
"Not here," she whispered.
It was whispered around the building that the merger had been signed weeks earlier.
The kids whispered through the entire ceremony.
He whispered a name I didn't catch and everyone else clearly did.

entries.patterns: yell + direct quotation / yell + that-clause / yell + wh-clause / yell + noun phrase (yelled a warning) / yell + at sb / yell + to sb / yell + at / to sb + to-infinitive / yell (intransitive)
entries.never: yell someone that / yell someone something
entries.meaning: Loud, usually angry speech. More informal and more emotional than shout — a coach shouts instructions and yells at a referee.
entries.transform: "Slow down! You're going to miss the turn!" -> She yelled at me to slow down.
examples: Somebody yelled that the last train was already on the platform.
She yelled to him from the top of the stairs and he never heard her.
Don't yell at the kid; he's four.
I got yelled at for something I hadn't done and apologized anyway.
He yelled until his voice gave out at the third quarter.
"Nobody's yelling," she said, yelling slightly.
